{{Expand Japanese}}
'''The Sengoku Period of Kinai and Neighboring Provinces''' (畿内・近国の戦国時代, *Kinai-Kingoku no Sengoku Jidai*) covers the Sengoku period of {{ill|Kinai|en|Kinai|qid=Q906708|lt=Kinai}} and its neighboring provinces, roughly corresponding to the modern {{ill|Kansai region|ar|منطقة كانساي|ast|Rexón de Kansai|az|Kansay regionu|azb|کانسای بؤلگه‌سی|ban|Wawengkon Kansai|be|Кансай|bn|কান্‌সাই অঞ্চল|ca|Kansai|ckb|ناوچەی کانسای|cs|Kansai|cy|Kansai|da|Kansai|de|Kinki|eo|Kansajo|es|Región de Kansai|et|Kansai|eu|Kansai eskualdea|fa|منطقه کانسای|fi|Kansai|fr|Région du Kansai|frr|Kansai|ga|Kansai|hak|Kinki|he|קנסאי|hi|कान्साइ क्षेत्र|hr|Kansai|hu|Kanszai|hy|Կինկի (տարածաշրջան)|id|Kansai|ilo|Rehion ti Kansai|is|Kansai|it|Kansai|ja|近畿地方|jv|Kansai|ka|კანსაი|ko|긴키 지방|lmo|Kansai|lt|Kansajo regionas|lv|Kansai reģions|mk|Кансај|mr|कन्साई|ms|Kawasan Kansai|my|ခန်းဆိုင်းဒေသ|nl|Kansai|nn|Kansai|no|Kansairegionen|os|Кансай|pam|Kansai labuad|pl|Region Kinki|pnb|کینسائی|pt|Kansai (região)|qu|Kansai suyu|ro|Regiunea Kansai|ru|Кансай|sc|Kansai|sco|Kansai|sd|ڪانسائي ريجن|sh|Kansai|si|කන්සායි කලාපය|simple|Kansai region|sk|Kansai|sl|Kansai|sr|Кансај|su|Wewengkon Kansai|sv|Kansai|th|คันไซ|tl|Rehiyon ng Kansai|tr|Kansai|uk|Регіон Кінкі|ur|کانسائی علاقہ|vi|Kinki|war|Kansai (rehiyon)|wuu|近畿地方|zh|近畿地方|zh_min_nan|Kinki tē-hng|zh_yue|近畿地方|qid=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}} during the late {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} and the [[Sengoku period (Japan)|Sengoku period]].

There are various theories regarding the chronological scope of the Sengoku period. This article follows the convention that defines its beginning with the [[Meiō Coup]] of {{ill|Meiō|en|Meiō|qid=Q1193841|lt=Meiō}} 2 (1493)<ref>Toriumi Toshiharu & [[Yumikura Hironori]], eds., ''The Sengoku Period of Southern Kinai'', [[Ebisukōshō Publishing]], 2017, p.1.</ref> and its end with the fall of the Muromachi shogunate in {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|en|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|qid=Q1145058|lt=Tenshō}} 1 (1573).<ref>Arimitsu Tomonori, ed., ''The Regional States of the Sengoku Period'', Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2003, p.71.</ref>

== Overview==
{{Double image aside|right|洛中洛外図左.jpg|300|洛中洛外図右.jpg|300|Scenes of Kyoto during the Eiroku era, from the [[Uesugi version of the Rakuchū Rakugai-zu]].}} 
{{After float}}

During the Sengoku period, Kinai was home to the capital city of {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, where the {{ill|Ashikaga shogunate|en|Ashikaga shogunate|qid=Q1154406|lt=Ashikaga shogunate}} ruled under the authority of the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|qid=Q208233|lt=Emperor}}, with the {{ill|Hosokawa clan|en|Hosokawa clan|qid=Q2736120|lt=Hosokawa clan}} serving as *{{ill|Kanrei|en|Kanrei|qid=Q1202497|lt=Kanrei}}* (Shogunal Deputy). Kinai consisted of five provinces: {{ill|Yamashiro Province|cs|Provincie Jamaširo|de|Provinz Yamashiro|es|Provincia de Yamashiro|fa|ولایت یاماشیرو|fr|Province de Yamashiro|gl|Provincia de Yamashiro|hak|Yamashiro-koet|id|Provinsi Yamashiro|it|Yamashiro (provincia)|ja|山城国|ko|야마시로국|lt|Jamaširo žemė|ms|Yamashiro Province|nl|Yamashiro (provincie)|pt|Província de Yamashiro|ru|Ямасиро (провинция)|simple|Yamashiro Province|sk|Jamaširo (provincia)|sr|Провинција Јамаширо|tr|Yamashiro (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Ямашіро|wuu|山城国|zh|山城國|zh_min_nan|Yamasiro-kok|zh_yue|山城國|qid=Q749276|lt=Yamashiro}}, home to Kyoto; {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|qid=Q907495|lt=Yamato}}, where the [[Kōfuku-ji]] temple held de facto {{ill|Shugo|en|Shugo|qid=Q1141023|lt=Shugo}} authority despite the absence of an official protector; {{ill|Settsu Province|ca|Província de Settsu|cs|Provincie Seccu|de|Provinz Settsu|eo|Provinco Seccu|es|Provincia de Settsu|fa|ولایت ستسو|fr|Province de Settsu|gl|Provincia de Settsu|hak|Settsu-koet|id|Provinsi Settsu|it|Settsu (provincia)|ja|摂津国|ko|셋쓰국|lt|Seccu žemė|nl|Settsu (provincie)|pt|Província de Settsu|ru|Сэтцу (провинция)|simple|Settsu Province|sk|Seccu (provincia)|sr|Провинција Сецу|tr|Settsu (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Сеццу|zh|攝津國|zh_min_nan|Settu-kok|zh_yue|攝津國|qid=Q864163|lt=Settsu}}, where the {{ill|Hongan-ji|en|Hongan-ji|qid=Q1627016|lt=Hongan-ji}} sect established its headquarters in Osaka during the [[Tenbun (era)|Tenbun era]]; {{ill|Izumi Province|en|Izumi Province|qid=Q1047117|lt=Izumi}}, home to the international trading port of {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|qid=Q193428|lt=Sakai}}; and {{ill|Kawachi Province|en|Kawachi Province|qid=Q1047150|lt=Kawachi}}, governed by the {{ill|Hatakeyama clan|en|Hatakeyama clan|qid=Q662881|lt=Hatakeyama clan}}, one of the {{ill|Kanrei|en|Kanrei|qid=Q1202497|lt=Three *Kanrei* Clans}}. These five provinces were collectively referred to as "*Tenka*" (天下, "the realm").<ref>[https://www.asahi.com/articles/ASN8225ZTN76PTJB010.html?iref=com_rnavi_aRank_nr05 'Was the Fall of Nobunaga’s Regime Due to Its Contradictions? Three New Theories Emerge'] - {{ill|The Asahi Shimbun|en|The Asahi Shimbun|qid=Q720503|lt=The Asahi Shimbun}}</ref> Additionally, nearby regions such as {{ill|Tanba Province|en|Tanba Province|qid=Q954511|lt=Tanba}}, which contained many {{ill|Imperial Court in Kyoto|en|Imperial Court in Kyoto|qid=Q11680900|lt=Imperial court}} and [[Kuge|noble]] estates, and {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|qid=Q843882|lt=Ōmi}}, controlled by the {{ill|Rokkaku clan|en|Rokkaku clan|qid=Q2975342|lt=Rokkaku clan}}, where the Ashikaga shoguns frequently sought refuge from conflicts in Kyoto, are also covered in this section.{{Efn|According to the ''Chronicle Summary'' (*Nendaiki Shōsetsu*), the scope of "*Tenka*" in *Eiroku* 11 (1568) included nine provinces: the five Kinai provinces plus [[Harima Province|Harima]] and [[Ise Province|Ise]].<ref>{{Cite journal|和書|author=Kuno Masashi |date=2020-03 |url=https://doi.org/10.34428/00013855 |title=The Kinai Rule of the Oda Nobunaga Regime |journal=Hakusan Shigaku |ISSN=0385-9460 |publisher=Hakusan Historical Society |volume=56 |pages=65-105 |doi=10.34428/00013855 |naid=40022207202 |CRID=1390294573746178432 |ref={{harvid|Kuno Masashi|2020b}}}} p.95</ref>.}}

The political landscape of Kinai and its neighboring provinces during the Sengoku period was marked by the spread of the conflict between {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshitane|en|Ashikaga Yoshitane|qid=Q708527|lt=Ashikaga Yoshitane}} and {{ill|Ashikaga Yoshizumi|en|Ashikaga Yoshizumi|qid=Q466281|lt=Ashikaga Yoshizumi}} in the Meiō-Eishō era,<ref>Matsushima Shūichi, "[https://hdl.handle.net/10424/4509 The Imagawa Clan and Western Mikawa in the Eishō Era]", ''Nihon Bunka Ronso'', Vol. 20, Aichi University, 2012, pp. 97-99, {{hdl|10424/4509}}</ref> and the ongoing struggle between the {{ill|Miyoshi clan|en|Miyoshi clan|qid=Q2975329|lt=Miyoshi clan}} and the shogunate during the Eiroku era, which created new political structures in the provinces.<ref>{{Cite journal|和書|author=Furuno Mitsugu, Murai Ryōsuke, Fujimoto Takahiro, Amano Tadayuki, Toriumi Toshiharu, Nishijima Tarō, Fujimoto Fumiko |date=2010-03 |url=https://doi.org/10.24544/ocu.20171213-107 |title=Reconstructing the Study of Kinai in the Sengoku Period and the 'Hosokawa Ryoke-ki' |journal=Urban Culture Research |ISSN=1348-3293 |publisher=Osaka City University Graduate School of Literature: Urban Culture Research Center |volume=12 |pages=159-178 |doi=10.24544/ocu.20171213-107 |naid=120006006922 |CRID=1390290699896202112}}</ref> These developments influenced not only Kinai and its neighboring provinces but also political movements across the entire Japanese archipelago.<ref>{{Cite |和書|author=Toriumi Toshiharu |date=2010-03 |url=https://www.lit.osaka-cu.ac.jp/UCRC/wp-content/uploads/2010/03/p159.pdf |format=PDF |title=Symposium: Reconstructing the Study of Kinai in the Sengoku Period and the 'Hosokawa Ryoke-ki' |chapter="Re-examining the Political History of the Sengoku Kinai through the Hatakeyama Clan" |journal=Urban Culture Research |ISSN=13483293 |publisher=Osaka City University Graduate School of Literature Urban Culture Research Center |issue=12 |pages=166-167 |CRID=1520853832233232128}}</ref> 

At the same time, regional [[Sengoku daimyō]] needed recognition from higher authorities to legitimize their rule, making connections with the Kyoto-based shogunate and Imperial Court indispensable.<ref>{{Cite journal|和書|author=Kobayashi Takehiko |date=1990-03 |url=https://glim-re.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/1533 |title=The Ōuchi Clan’s Policy Toward Kyoto: Focusing on the Role of Resident Agents (Monks) |journal=Gakushūin Shigaku |ISSN=02861658 |publisher=Gakushūin University Historical Society |issue=28 |page=17 |hdl=10959/1810 |CRID=1050564288171432704}}</ref><ref name=Imaoka>{{Cite journal|和書|author=Imaoka Norikazu |date=2009-03 |url=https://kusw.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/10 |title=Shugo Authority During the Sengoku Period: The Case of the Asakura Clan in Echizen |journal=Kansai Welfare University Bulletin of Social Welfare Studies |ISSN=1883566X |publisher=Kansai Welfare University |issue=12 |page=59 |naid=40016560024 |CRID=1050282812568651520}}</ref> Additionally, Kyoto often became a battleground for regional daimyō disputes, such as in the [[Yōkyūkai Incident]], highlighting the pivotal role of Kinai and its surrounding provinces in shaping the broader history of Sengoku Japan.
